strengths: The proposed RCPU method is technically sound: the rotation-constrained compensation is formulated cleanly as an Orthogonal Procrustes problem with a well-known closed-form solution, and the paper correctly derives both the rotation and scaled variants (Eq. 5-9).

The motivation is clearly articulated: unconstrained least-squares fitting can overfit to small calibration sets and distort representation geometry, and constraining to rotations reduces effective degrees of freedom. The empirical comparison against LS compensation in Figure 2 directly supports this claim.

Experiments include both perplexity and a suite of seven zero-shot benchmarks, with consistent improvements over WANDA-sp and mostly over FLAP, particularly at higher pruning ratios (e.g., PPL 18.21 vs 18.59 at 30%).

Useful ablations are provided, including where to apply the compensation (o_proj vs down_proj, Table 3) and an efficiency analysis (Table 4) that honestly discusses the counter-intuitive pruning-time trend.
The method is plug-in, requires no architectural changes, no fine-tuning, and is computationally cheap (~10s per layer), making it practically relevant.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core technique is the classical Orthogonal Procrustes solution (Golub & Van Loan, 2013) applied per layer; the variance-aware score is a minor modification of the WANDA-sp score (adding one multiplicative variance term). The technical contribution is incremental.

Evaluation scope is narrow: only LLaMA-7B is evaluated. No results on other model families (LLaMA-2/3, Mistral, Qwen) or model sizes, which is a significant concern for a paper claiming practical applicability to 'large-scale deployments'.

Missing baselines: no quantitative comparison with SliceGPT despite substantial discussion in related work, nor with other training-free structured pruning methods or a least-squares variant with regularization/low-rank constraints, which would clarify whether rotation is truly the best-constrained family.

No ablation on calibration set size, and no analysis of variance across calibration seeds; given that the central claim is about statistical stability under limited calibration, this directly relevant experiment is absent.

Benchmark gains over FLAP are modest and mixed (e.g., mean accuracy 56.34 vs 56.20 at 30%; several individual tasks are worse at 10%), and no statistical significance or variance reporting is provided for these small margins.

The claim that rotation preserves geometry 'avoiding overfitting' is asserted theoretically but only weakly validated; there is no analysis of output norm/inner-product preservation or generalization gap to substantiate the mechanism.

No code release or reproducibility statement is mentioned; several implementation details (e.g., which layers are pruned simultaneously, exact score normalization) would be needed to reproduce results.

Writing has minor issues (e.g., 'a rotation matrix', 'an original linear map'), and Table 1 presents only WikiText-2 PPL with no other language-modeling evaluation (e.g., C4) to check calibration-set overfitting on the evaluation distribution itself.

strengths: The paper is clearly written and the core idea — formulating post-pruning error compensation as an Orthogonal Procrustes problem with a closed-form SVD solution — is simple, well-motivated, and easy to implement on top of existing column-pruning pipelines.

The variance-aware pruning score is a reasonable, if incremental, extension of the WANDA-sp heuristic, and the ablation in Table 3 (where to apply the rotation) and the score/update decomposition in Figure 2 provide some useful empirical insight.
The paper includes practical efficiency measurements (parameter counts, memory, per-layer pruning time) and discusses a GPU-related counter-intuitive timing trend honestly.
The method requires no retraining or architectural changes, which is practically attractive for post-training structured pruning.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: applying Orthogonal Procrustes to align two feature sets is a textbook technique (Golub & Van Loan, 2013), and the paper is essentially 'run one SVD per layer after WANDA-sp/FLAP-style column pruning'. The variance-aware score adds one multiplicative factor to an existing score. The conceptual contribution is thin for a top-tier venue.

Narrow and weak evaluation: experiments are conducted only on LLaMA-7B at 10-30% pruning of o_proj and down_proj. No LLaMA-2/3, Vicuna, or other model families, no other sub-layer types (q/k/v_proj, gate/up_proj), and no comparison to SliceGPT or LLM-Pruner, despite SliceGPT being an orthogonal-rotation-based structured pruning method that is discussed at length in related work.

The baseline comparison is incomplete: FLAP and WANDA-sp are the only baselines. The unconstrained least-squares update is evaluated (Figure 2) but never in the main tables, and stronger recent structured pruning methods are missing, making it hard to judge whether RCPU is actually competitive.

The headline gains are modest and inconsistent: mean zero-shot accuracy at 10% pruning is 64.01 (RCPU) vs 63.80 (FLAP), and per-task results are mixed (e.g., RCPU loses clearly to FLAP on BoolQ and ARC at 30% with the Rot. variant). No variance/significance analysis over seeds or calibration sets is provided, so claims of 'consistently better' accuracy are not fully supported.

The theoretical motivation is largely hand-wavy: claims that unconstrained least squares 'overfits and destructively modifies pretrained weights' and that rotation constraints 'improve statistical stability' are asserted but never analyzed (no generalization argument, no conditioning/variance analysis, no experiments on calibration-set size to substantiate the overfitting story).

A methodological concern: the Procrustes rotation acts on the dout×dout output space, but the pruning error Y - W_K X_K contains the unrecoverable term W_D X_D; a pure rotation cannot represent arbitrary corrections to it, and the paper does not analyze when or why the rotation should help, beyond intuition about 'principal directions'.

No code or reproducibility artifacts are mentioned, and details that matter (e.g., handling of RMSNorm/residual connections, sequential vs. parallel propagation of updated activations to later layers, calibration hyperparameters) are underspecified.
The scaled variant (Rot.+Scale) adds essentially nothing per the authors' own results and discussion, further diluting the contribution.

strengths: Clear and well-structured problem formulation: the paper precisely decomposes the post-pruning error (Eq. 1-3) and motivates constraining the compensation map, making the method easy to follow and reproduce conceptually.

The core method is clean and principled: formulating post-pruning error compensation as an Orthogonal Procrustes problem yields a closed-form solution (SVD-based) with negligible overhead, and it can be plugged directly after Wanda-sp style column pruning without architectural changes.

The ablations are informative and well-executed: the study of where to apply the rotation (Table 3, o_proj vs down_proj vs both) and the honest analysis of the counter-intuitive timing trend (tall-skinny GEMM inefficiency) show genuine scientific engagement with the results.

Empirical gains over both WANDA-sp and FLAP are consistent on WikiText-2 perplexity and mean zero-shot accuracy across pruning ratios, and the benefit grows at higher sparsity, supporting the central claim.
The decomposition of pruning score vs. compensation method (Figure 2) is a useful experimental design that isolates the contribution of the variance-aware score from the rotation update.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the core technique is the classical Orthogonal Procrustes solution (Golub & Van Loan, 2013) applied layerwise after an existing pruning score. The variance-aware importance score is a one-factor extension of Wanda-sp. Both components are individually straightforward, and the contribution is primarily an empirical combination rather than a new methodological idea.

Narrow evaluation: experiments are restricted to a single model (original LLaMA-7B, not Llama-2/3 or other families such as Qwen or Mistral), a single calibration dataset (WikiText-2, 128 samples), and only one calibration set size. There is no C4 perplexity, no other model scales, and no code release mentioned, limiting both generality claims and reproducibility.

Weak baseline coverage: only WANDA-sp and FLAP are compared. Other relevant structured, training-free baselines (e.g., SliceGPT, structured variants of SparseGPT, LLM-Pruner without fine-tuning, BLP) are discussed in related work but not evaluated, making it hard to judge competitiveness against the broader state of the art.

The central argument about overfitting of unconstrained least-squares is asserted more than demonstrated: there is no controlled evidence (e.g., varying calibration set size, held-out calibration data, or analysis of the LS solution's condition number) to confirm that LS failure is due to overfitting rather than distribution shift or error accumulation across layers. The degrees-of-freedom argument is also weak: a full rotation retains d(d-1)/2 DOF, only about half of a general linear map, and a dense rotation still mixes all output coordinates, which sits uneasily with the paper's own 'undesired coupling' desideratum (Section 2.2, point iii).

Some claims overstate the evidence: 'consistently better perplexity and task accuracy compared with existing baselines' is not fully supported since RCPU (Rot.) is sometimes second-best to FLAP per task (e.g., ARC-e at 10%), improvements at 10% pruning on benchmarks are marginal (64.01 vs 63.80 mean), and the scaled variant's benefit is within noise. The theoretical justification for why the variance term in the score aligns with principal output directions is intuitive rather than derived.
Statistical rigor is missing: no error bars, seeds, or significance tests are reported for perplexity or accuracy, which matters given the small margins between methods at lower pruning ratios.

strengths: The paper is well written and clearly organized; the core method (post-pruning compensation as an Orthogonal Procrustes problem with a closed-form SVD solution) is simple, hyperparameter-free, and easy to reproduce conceptually.

The evaluation is reasonably thorough for the scope: two model families (Llama-7B/2-13B, Vicuna-7B), three pruning ratios (10/20/30%), two calibration sizes (128/512), perplexity plus seven zero-shot benchmarks, and additional baselines (Wanda-sp, FLAP, SliceGPT, LS+Ridge).

The paper is honest about limitations: it shows that LS+Ridge with oracle λ can match or beat RCPU in PPL at N_calib=512, and provides a useful sensitivity analysis of λ (Appendix 7.4) rather than hiding unfavorable results.

Good ablations: where to apply compensation (o_proj vs down_proj vs both), score-with/without compensation comparisons (Figure 3), variance-aware score vs Wanda-sp score, scaled vs rotation-only variant, and runtime/complexity analysis.
The contrast with LS fitting under small calibration sets is a sensible, well-motivated observation, supported by a DoF-style argument and empirical instability of Ridge λ selection.
weaknesses: Limited novelty. The central technique is the classical Orthogonal Procrustes solution (Golub & Van Loan), applied as a one-line post-processing step after column pruning; the variance-aware score is a small extension of the Wanda-sp heuristic. The contribution is essentially a combination of well-known components, and the paper itself positions RCPU as close to FLAP.

Gains over baselines are modest and not always consistent. On several settings FLAP or Wanda-sp wins individual tasks (e.g., Table 2 at 30%: FLAP mean 56.20 vs RCPU 55.50/56.34; SliceGPT beats RCPU on ARC-e/ARC-c at 10% in Table 3), and the PPL advantage over FLAP is often within ~0.1-0.5. The claimed 'consistently better' headline overstates the evidence.

Theoretical support is thin and partly hand-wavy. The claim that high-variance inputs 'align with dominant output directions' and hence should be kept is a heuristic assertion without analysis or direct measurement; the degree-of-freedom comparison between ridge and per-layer rotations (5.36e8 vs 1.4e9) is informal and not an apples-to-apples argument for generalization.

Narrow evaluation scope: only Llama-1/2-era and Vicuna models; no Llama-3, Mistral, Qwen, or larger models; no wall-clock inference speedup measurements (only parameter/memory counts), so the practical acceleration benefit of structured pruning is not directly demonstrated.

Reproducibility is weakened by an incomplete footnote ('Codes are available at' with no URL), and the reproducibility statement claims settings are fully described while some details (e.g., exact seed handling, variance definitions, calibration token sampling) are spread out or missing.

Some inconsistencies between reported numbers (e.g., Table 1 RCPU 10% N_calib=128 is 13.55/13.52 while Table 4 'both updated' at 10% is 13.55 — fine — but the relation between Figure 3's uncompensated bars and Table 1 baseline rows is not always clearly traceable), and bold/underline conventions are occasionally confusing (Table 1, 10% row).

The scaled variant is reported throughout but the paper itself concludes it brings negligible benefit, adding clutter rather than insight; a tighter version focused on the main result would be stronger.

strengths: The core method is simple, clean, and fully specified: post-pruning error compensation is cast as a classical Orthogonal Procrustes problem with a closed-form SVD solution, making the method hyperparameter-free (in contrast to Ridge regularization, whose λ must be tuned), which is a practical advantage for LLM pruning.

The experimental protocol is reasonably thorough for a method paper: two model families plus Vicuna, two calibration sizes (128/512), three pruning ratios, PPL and seven zero-shot benchmarks, and useful ablations (which sub-layers to compensate, LS+Ridge vs RCPU, λ sensitivity analysis in the appendix).
The paper is honest about unfavorable results: LS compensation overtakes RCPU in PPL at N_calib=512, and the scaled variant yields only marginal gains; these are reported rather than hidden.
The proposed compensation is a drop-in module after Wanda-sp-style column pruning with modest overhead (~9s per layer) and no architectural changes, so it is easily reproducible and composable.

The empirical claim that rotation-constrained updates generalize better than unconstrained LS fits to downstream tasks (even when LS wins on calibration-adjacent PPL) is an interesting and potentially useful observation.
weaknesses: Limited novelty: the central contribution is applying the textbook Orthogonal Procrustes solution to post-pruning weight updates, plus a small heuristic modification of the Wanda-sp importance score (multiplying by input variance). The related work already contains several rotation-based pruning methods (SliceGPT, RotPruner, DenoiseRotator), and the paper's positioning relative to them is thin.

The theoretical motivation is heuristic rather than rigorous. The 'preserving geometry prevents overfitting' narrative is intuitive but unproven; the degrees-of-freedom comparison (d_out(d_out-1)/2 vs. ridge's effective dof) is a loose analogy — a full-rank orthogonal matrix chosen to minimize calibration error does not obviously have 'small dof' in a statistically meaningful sense, and this argument is not validated empirically.

Improvement magnitudes are small and inconsistent: e.g., mean accuracy gains over FLAP are often ~0.2–1.5 points, in some settings FLAP ties or wins (Table 2, 20%: RCPU 61.57 vs FLAP 61.32; Table 3, 10%: Wanda-sp mean 67.78 close to RCPU 67.95). No confidence intervals, seeds, or statistical significance tests are reported, so whether these gains exceed noise is unclear.

The evaluation scope is narrow: only Llama-family and Vicuna models, WikiText-2 perplexity, and standard zero-shot benchmarks; no inference latency/throughput measurements of the actually pruned models; no comparison to several recent structured pruning approaches beyond FLAP/SliceGPT/Wanda-sp.

A clean ablation isolating the variance term in the scoring rule (proposed score vs. Wanda-sp score under identical compensation) is only partially presented via Figure 3 bar charts without numerical values, making the individual contribution of the score component hard to assess.

Reproducibility is weakened: the code availability footnote is effectively empty ('Codes are available at' with no link), and the appendix sections 7.3 and beyond contain tables without accompanying discussion.

Writing quality issues: several grammatical errors and awkward phrasings ('orthogonal matrices' in Sec 4.3, 'changes the module to apply'), Figure 2/3 legends and caption mismatches, and the claim that RCPU 'consistently' improves over FLAP is overstated given near-ties in multiple settings.

strengths: The core idea is clean and well-motivated: formulating post-pruning error compensation as an Orthogonal Procrustes problem gives a closed-form, hyperparameter-free update that preserves output geometry, in contrast to Ridge-regularized least-squares fitting which the paper convincingly shows can overfit or destabilize with small calibration sets (Figures 5-6, Section 7.4).

The experimental protocol is more thorough than typical pruning papers: two calibration sizes (128/512), multiple pruning ratios, three models (Llama-7B, Llama-2-13B, Vicuna-7B), seven zero-shot benchmarks, and useful ablations including which sub-layers to compensate (Table 4) and sensitivity of the Ridge baseline to lambda.

The claim that rotation-constrained updates are more robust under limited calibration is supported by the degree-of-freedom comparison and the observed instability of LS+Ridge at small Ncalib, and RCPU consistently beats LS compensation on downstream tasks even when LS wins on calibration PPL.
The method is plug-in and practical: no architectural changes, ~10s per layer, and the variance-aware score is a natural, sensible extension of the Wanda-sp score.
The paper is clearly written, positioning against FLAP, SliceGPT, Wanda-sp, and rotation-based pruners (RotPruner, DenoiseRotator) is adequate, and code availability is promised.
weaknesses: Limited novelty. The core technique is a textbook Orthogonal Procrustes solution (SVD of YZ^T) applied per layer after column pruning. The variance-aware score is an incremental modification of the Wanda-sp heuristic. The contribution is an application/twist of a classical closed-form method rather than a new technique, which weakens the case for a top-tier venue.

Improvements over the strongest baseline (FLAP) are modest and not uniform. PPL gains are often under one point, and on downstream accuracy RCPU sometimes loses to simpler baselines (e.g., WANDA-sp 67.74 vs RCPU 67.18 mean on Llama-2-13B at 10%/128 in Table 7; several per-task losses in Tables 2-3). No variance across seeds or significance testing is reported, so small margins are hard to interpret.

Missing evaluation of the actual practical benefit. The stated motivation is deployment efficiency, yet the paper reports only parameter count and memory, not wall-clock latency, throughput, or FLOPs reduction of the pruned models, which is the metric that matters for structured pruning claims.

Baseline coverage is narrow. Missing recent and competitive structured pruning methods without retraining (e.g., ECoFLaP, LoSparse variants, LLM-Pruner-style pipelines with lightweight recovery, BESA) would strengthen the comparison. SliceGPT is only compared at 13B.

The theoretical justification is informal. The overfitting argument for rotations is intuitive but not formalized; the degrees-of-freedom comparison between Ridge and orthogonal constraints is crude (Q has dout(dout-1)/2 DOF but is data-dependent, so this is not directly comparable as written), and there is no analysis of how per-layer rotations interact or accumulate across the network beyond qualitative discussion.

Evaluation is restricted to Llama-family 7B/13B models, WikiText-2-only calibration, and multiple-choice benchmarks via the Harness; no generative or instruction-following evaluation despite the stated deployment motivation.

Some presentation issues: Table 1 is labeled 'representative' PPL without clarifying the selection; the counter-intuitive pruning-time trend (Section 4.4/5) is explained by GPU library behavior rather than measured profiling; Figure 1 is only schematic.
